questions.title: @SpringBootTest
questions.question: What is @SpringBootTest and when should you use it?

sections.title: What the Interviewer Wants to Hear
sections.content:
- **Loads full application context:** includes all auto-configurations and beans
- **`webEnvironment`:** NONE, MOCK, RANDOM_PORT, DEFINED_PORT — know all four
- **Integration test, not unit test:** it's slow — use only when you need the full context
- **Starts the embedded server:** with `RANDOM_PORT` or `DEFINED_PORT`
- **Red flag:** using `@SpringBootTest` for every test — shows lack of judgment about test scope

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
`@SpringBootTest` loads the complete Spring application context — all your beans, auto-configurations, and the embedded server if you choose. It's the annotation for integration tests where you need to verify that components work together correctly.

The `webEnvironment` attribute controls the server setup. `MOCK` — the default — creates a mock servlet environment without starting a real HTTP server, used with `MockMvc`. `RANDOM_PORT` starts a real embedded server on a random port — use `@LocalServerPort` to inject the actual port. `NONE` loads the context without any web environment.

The key judgment call is when to use `@SpringBootTest`. It's slower than focused slice tests because it loads everything. Use it when you're testing cross-cutting concerns, database interactions end-to-end, or HTTP layer integration. For testing just the web layer, use `@WebMvcTest`. For just the data layer, use `@DataJpaTest`. Don't use `@SpringBootTest` by default for every test.

sections.title: Concept Explained

speakable_v2.hook: @SpringBootTest loads the complete Spring application context — all your beans, auto-configurations, and the embedded server if you choose.
speakable_v2.cap: Don't use @SpringBootTest by default for every test.

questions.title: @WebMvcTest
questions.question: What is @WebMvcTest and how does it differ from @SpringBootTest?

sections.title: What the Interviewer Wants to Hear
sections.content:
- **Slice test:** only loads MVC components — controllers, filters, `@ControllerAdvice`, converters
- **Does NOT load:** services, repositories, `@Component` beans — must mock them
- **`MockMvc` auto-configured:** the only way to send requests in a `@WebMvcTest`
- **Security is loaded:** Spring Security configuration applies — often needs `@WithMockUser`
- **Red flag:** not knowing why services must be mocked — shows misunderstanding of what's in the slice

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
`@WebMvcTest` is a focused slice test that loads only the Spring MVC layer — your controllers, request mappers, exception handlers, filters, and JSON converters. Services, repositories, and other non-web beans are not loaded, which makes it significantly faster than `@SpringBootTest`.

Because services aren't loaded, you must mock them with `@MockBean`. The test auto-configures `MockMvc`, which you use to send HTTP requests and assert on responses — no real server starts.

One important gotcha: Spring Security IS loaded in `@WebMvcTest` by default. If your controller has security, requests will be blocked unless you configure security for the test. The simplest approaches are `@WithMockUser` from Spring Security test support, or `@WithUserDetails` for user-specific scenarios. You can also use `@WebMvcTest(excludeAutoConfiguration = SecurityAutoConfiguration.class)` to disable security entirely for tests that don't need it.

sections.title: Concept Explained

speakable_v2.hook: @WebMvcTest is a focused slice test that loads only the Spring MVC layer — your controllers, request mappers, exception handlers, filters, and JSON converters.

beats.text: The production failure mode here is unchecked state mutation under concurrent access.

speakable_v2.cap: You can also use @WebMvcTest(excludeAutoConfiguration = SecurityAutoConfiguration.class) to disable security entirely for tests that don't need it.

questions.title: @DataJpaTest
questions.question: What is @DataJpaTest and what does it configure?

sections.title: What the Interviewer Wants to Hear
sections.content:
- **Slice test for persistence layer:** loads JPA repositories, `EntityManager`, and data sources
- **In-memory H2 by default:** replaces real database — auto-configured with `create-drop` schema
- **`@Transactional`:** tests roll back after each test method by default
- **`TestEntityManager`:** helper for setting up test data without going through repositories
- **Red flag:** not knowing it rolls back — tests should work in any order

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
`@DataJpaTest` is a persistence slice test that loads only the JPA layer — repositories, `EntityManager`, Hibernate, and the data source. It does not load your services or controllers. By default, it configures an in-memory H2 database and sets `ddl-auto=create-drop` so the schema is created from your entities and dropped after the test.

Each test method runs in a transaction that rolls back at the end. This gives test isolation — data inserted in one test doesn't leak into another. You don't have to clean up test data manually.

`TestEntityManager` is the recommended way to set up test data. It wraps the JPA `EntityManager` with test-friendly methods like `persistAndFlush` that save an entity and immediately flush to the database, ensuring queries in the same transaction see the persisted data. Test methods then exercise the actual repository methods and assert on results.

sections.title: Concept Explained

speakable_v2.hook: @DataJpaTest is a persistence slice test that loads only the JPA layer — repositories, EntityManager, Hibernate, and the data source.
speakable_v2.cap: Test methods then exercise the actual repository methods and assert on results.

questions.title: @MockBean and @SpyBean
questions.question: What are @MockBean and @SpyBean and when do you use each?

sections.title: What the Interviewer Wants to Hear
sections.content:
- **`@MockBean`:** replaces a Spring bean with a Mockito mock — no real implementation
- **`@SpyBean`:** wraps real bean with Mockito spy — real methods called unless stubbed
- **Context reset:** both cause a new application context — use sparingly
- **`@MockBean` vs `@Mock`:** `@MockBean` is Spring-aware and wired into the context; `@Mock` is plain Mockito
- **Red flag:** using `@MockBean` in every test class — shows context caching ignorance

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
`@MockBean` adds a Mockito mock of a bean to the Spring application context, replacing any existing bean of the same type. All methods on the mock return default values — null for objects, 0 for primitives, empty collections — unless you stub them with `given()`. Use it when you want to test a component in isolation from its dependencies.

`@SpyBean` wraps the actual Spring bean with a Mockito spy. Real methods are called by default — you only stub the specific interactions you want to control. Use it when you want most of the real behaviour but need to verify specific method calls were made, or need to override a specific method.

Both have an important performance implication: adding `@MockBean` or `@SpyBean` to a test class forces Spring to create a new application context for that test class, because the context's bean registry has changed. This breaks context caching and slows down your test suite. Centralise `@MockBean` declarations into a shared base class or configuration where possible.

sections.title: Concept Explained

speakable_v2.hook: @MockBean adds a Mockito mock of a bean to the Spring application context, replacing any existing bean of the same type.
speakable_v2.cap: Centralise @MockBean declarations into a shared base class or configuration where possible.

questions.title: MockMvc
questions.question: How do you use MockMvc to test Spring MVC controllers?

sections.title: What the Interviewer Wants to Hear
sections.content:
- **No real HTTP:** MockMvc dispatches requests directly to the DispatcherServlet in-process
- **Fluent builder API:** `perform()`, `andExpect()`, `andDo()`, `andReturn()`
- **Common matchers:** `status()`, `jsonPath()`, `content()`, `header()`
- **`perform(post(...).content(json))`:** sending a request body requires content type + body
- **Red flag:** using `andReturn()` when dedicated matchers exist — chaining expectations is cleaner

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
MockMvc tests the Spring MVC layer without starting a real HTTP server. It dispatches requests directly through the DispatcherServlet in the same JVM thread, so it's fast and gives you full access to the Spring context during the request lifecycle — exception handling, content negotiation, validation, and response serialisation all happen as they would in production.

The API is fluent: you call `mockMvc.perform(request)` then chain `.andExpect()` matchers and optionally `.andDo()` for side effects like printing the response. Common matchers are `status().isOk()` or `status().is(200)`, `jsonPath("$.field").value("expected")`, `content().contentType(MediaType.APPLICATION_JSON)`, and `header().exists("Location")`.

For POST requests with a body, you need to set the content type and provide the serialised body: `.content(objectMapper.writeValueAsString(request)).contentType(MediaType.APPLICATION_JSON)`.

speakable_v2.hook: MockMvc tests the Spring MVC layer without starting a real HTTP server.

beats.text: The production failure mode here is unchecked state mutation under concurrent access.

speakable_v2.cap: For POST requests with a body, you need to set the content type and provide the serialised body: .content(objectMapper.writeValueAsString(request)).contentType(MediaType.APPLICATION_JSON).

questions.title: TestRestTemplate
questions.question: What is TestRestTemplate and how is it different from MockMvc?

sections.title: What the Interviewer Wants to Hear
sections.content:
- **Real HTTP:** TestRestTemplate sends actual HTTP requests to the started server
- **Requires `RANDOM_PORT` or `DEFINED_PORT`:** needs a real server running
- **Fault-tolerant by default:** doesn't throw on 4xx/5xx — check `ResponseEntity.getStatusCode()`
- **MockMvc is for slice tests, TestRestTemplate for full integration tests:** know the trade-off
- **Red flag:** using TestRestTemplate in a `@WebMvcTest` — no real server there

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
`TestRestTemplate` makes real HTTP requests to an embedded server running in your test. It's auto-configured by Spring Boot when you use `@SpringBootTest(webEnvironment = RANDOM_PORT)`. Unlike `MockMvc`, which dispatches directly through the DispatcherServlet in-process, `TestRestTemplate` goes through the full network stack — actual serialization, deserialization, and HTTP.

By default, `TestRestTemplate` is fault-tolerant: it doesn't throw exceptions on 4xx or 5xx responses. Instead, you check `ResponseEntity.getStatusCode()`. This is intentional — you often want to assert on error responses without catching exceptions.

The key difference from MockMvc in practice: `TestRestTemplate` gives you more confidence because it exercises the full stack including Tomcat's request handling, security filters, and actual HTTP headers. MockMvc is faster and works with `@WebMvcTest`. For verifying complete end-to-end HTTP contracts, `TestRestTemplate` is more appropriate.

sections.title: Concept Explained

speakable_v2.hook: TestRestTemplate makes real HTTP requests to an embedded server running in your test.
speakable_v2.cap: For verifying complete end-to-end HTTP contracts, TestRestTemplate is more appropriate.

questions.title: Testcontainers Integration
questions.question: How do you use Testcontainers for integration testing with real databases?

sections.title: What the Interviewer Wants to Hear
sections.content:
- **Starts Docker containers for tests:** real PostgreSQL, Redis, RabbitMQ — not mocks
- **`@Container` + static field:** container shared across all tests in the class
- **`@DynamicPropertySource`:** injects container's port/URL into Spring's property source
- **`@Testcontainers`:** class-level annotation enabling the extension
- **Red flag:** not knowing the port is dynamic — hardcoding the port defeats the purpose

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
Testcontainers is a Java library that programmatically starts Docker containers in your tests and cleans them up afterward. Instead of connecting to a shared test database or using H2 as a substitute, your integration tests get a real PostgreSQL — or Redis, or Kafka — on an ephemeral port.

You annotate the test class with `@Testcontainers`, declare a `static` `@Container` field with the container configuration, and use `@DynamicPropertySource` to inject the container's dynamic port and connection URL into Spring's property sources. Spring Boot then uses these properties when configuring the data source.

The key insight is why static: a static container is started once before all test methods and stopped after the last one. This makes the test suite much faster — starting a PostgreSQL container takes 2-3 seconds, so you pay that cost once per class, not once per test.

sections.title: Concept Explained

speakable_v2.hook: Testcontainers is a Java library that programmatically starts Docker containers in your tests and cleans them up afterward.
speakable_v2.cap: This makes the test suite much faster — starting a PostgreSQL container takes 2-3 seconds, so you pay that cost once per class, not once per test.

questions.title: Test Slices Overview
questions.question: What are the main Spring Boot test slices and when do you use each?

sections.title: What the Interviewer Wants to Hear
sections.content:
- **Slice = partial application context:** only loads components relevant to one layer
- **Main slices:** `@WebMvcTest`, `@DataJpaTest`, `@JsonTest`, `@RestClientTest`
- **Why slices matter:** faster than full context, focused failures
- **Trade-off:** must mock cross-layer dependencies
- **Red flag:** only knowing `@SpringBootTest` — shows no experience with structured test layering

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
Spring Boot test slices let you test one layer of your application in isolation without loading the entire context. Each slice annotation loads only the beans relevant to that layer.

`@WebMvcTest` loads controllers, filters, and security — for testing HTTP endpoints. `@DataJpaTest` loads repositories, the entity manager, and a database — for testing persistence. `@JsonTest` loads JSON serialization/deserialization only — for testing your Jackson configuration and custom serializers. `@RestClientTest` loads `RestTemplate` and `@Service` beans that make HTTP calls — for testing outbound HTTP clients.

The strategy is to use the narrowest slice that covers what you're testing. A controller test doesn't need a database; a repository test doesn't need a web layer. Slices run faster, fail more precisely, and are easier to set up because you mock fewer things.

sections.title: Concept Explained

speakable_v2.hook: Spring Boot test slices let you test one layer of your application in isolation without loading the entire context.
speakable_v2.cap: Slices run faster, fail more precisely, and are easier to set up because you mock fewer things.

questions.title: Test Property Configuration
questions.question: How do you configure properties specifically for tests?

sections.title: What the Interviewer Wants to Hear
sections.content:
- **`@TestPropertySource`:** class-level, can point to a file or inline properties
- **`@SpringBootTest(properties=...)`:** inline, test-class scoped
- **`application-test.properties`:** profile-based, loaded with `@ActiveProfiles("test")`
- **`@DynamicPropertySource`:** programmatic, for dynamic values like container ports
- **Red flag:** hardcoding test values directly in code instead of externalising to properties

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
There are four main ways to provide test-specific properties, each suited to a different scenario.

`@TestPropertySource(locations = "classpath:test-overrides.properties")` points to a specific properties file and is applied at the class level. `@SpringBootTest(properties = {"key=value"})` inlines properties directly in the annotation — good for a single override without creating a separate file. `application-test.properties` plus `@ActiveProfiles("test")` is the standard approach for broad test configuration that multiple test classes share.

`@DynamicPropertySource` is a method-level annotation for programmatic registration — essential for Testcontainers where you don't know the container's port until runtime. You can't put a dynamic port in a static properties file, so `@DynamicPropertySource` fills that gap.

speakable_v2.cap: You can't put a dynamic port in a static properties file, so @DynamicPropertySource fills that gap.

questions.title: Transactional Test Isolation
questions.question: How does @Transactional work in tests and why does it matter?

sections.title: What the Interviewer Wants to Hear
sections.content:
- **Auto-rollback:** `@Transactional` on test class causes each test to roll back after completion
- **`@DataJpaTest` applies this by default:** know why
- **`@Commit`:** override for a specific test when you need the data to persist
- **Caveat:** doesn't work for methods that require their own new transaction
- **Red flag:** assuming transactional rollback makes `TRUNCATE` or manual cleanup unnecessary in all scenarios

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
When you annotate a test class or method with `@Transactional`, Spring wraps each test method in a transaction and rolls it back after the method completes. This is the default behaviour in `@DataJpaTest` and it's the reason repository tests have isolation without explicit cleanup — every INSERT, UPDATE, or DELETE in the test is undone before the next test runs.

The rollback is why test methods can be run in any order without side effects. One test can insert a user, assert on it, and the next test starts with the same clean state.

The caveat is methods that use `@Transactional(propagation = REQUIRES_NEW)`. These create a new transaction independent of the test transaction, so they commit even though the outer test transaction rolls back. Tests for these methods must do their own cleanup or use a different isolation strategy like `@Sql` with `executionPhase = AFTER_TEST_METHOD`.
